title: Majestic Knishop
reviewNotes: Two branches, six exact positions from the supported seven-piece finish after ...Qxd7 at 121s. Earlier nine-/eight-piece knight route and bishop sacrifice are source context, not certified here. Nb6+ forks Ka4/Qd7; source ...Ka3 and independent ...Kb5 both allow Nxd7 with a checked win requiring conversion.
transcript: White's brilliant idea is B4 check, now forcing the king to move. But if the king goes to B5, now there [music] is going to be a skewer with the bishop picking up the queen and winning the game. And if the king goes to A4, thinking that he's now safe, white is going to follow up with knight to B2 check, pushing the king even further down the board. But don't forget that black has a full extra queen, and so it's going to be pretty easy for him to escape all of these threats and eventually win the game. Or at least that's what you would think. But white has a brilliant idea in this position. White continues with knight to C4 check. Now the king cannot go to any of these squares, so it's forced to go back up to A4. Now we would have the option of repeating moves and getting at least a draw, but white is trying to achieve something far more valuable. So white plays knight takes B6 check, now picking up a fundamental pawn. Black never really wants to give up a queen for a knight, and remember you can never go here because of the bishop skewer. So the black king will have to go back. And now it might seem like black is out of the woods. There is no continuation for white. Despite the two passed pawns, the black queen is going to be able to stop them. But white is not a fool, and he knows that there's something here. And so he plays knight back to C4. What can possibly be the idea? Well, the king has to come back up, and now white plays the very mysterious and quiet move bishop to F5. After all of those knight checks, we have come to a position where the bishop is threatening to give a checkmate in one move. And that is the reason why we needed to pick up the black pawn, because otherwise black would have the option to push that pawn now and close the diagonal. But there's no need for that, right? The black queen can just cover from D7, and now there's not going to be any checkmate. But whenever you're evaluating a threat and your opponent stops it, you need to ask yourself, what would happen if I do it anyway? And bishop to D7 is the way to win this game, because this would be a checkmate if it wasn't for the fact that the queen can take the bishop. But now, we have successfully placed the queen and king in the perfect position to deliver this knight fork. And we're going to pick up the queen and win the game.
